items.text: YOUR BROWSER IS ABOUT TO GET BUSY.
FILES ARE NOT YET A PAGE.
A FRAME IS AN ENGINEERED RESULT.
GREAT EXPERIENCES MAKE COMPLEXITY FEEL SIMPLE.

scenes.narration: You press Enter. One tiny action starts a chain of events your eyes will never see.
First, the browser needs an IP address. DNS translates names; a cached answer can make this step disappear.
Requests travel through networks as packets. Routers forward them toward their destination, one hop at a time.
For HTTPS, the browser checks the site's identity and establishes encryption before exchanging protected application data.
The browser sends an HTTP request: which resource it needs, and the information the server needs to respond.
A server may return a prepared file, query a database, or run application logic to create a response.
A nearby cache may already hold reusable content. Less distance and less work can mean a faster answer.
The response can contain HTML, styles, scripts and images. But none of those files is the finished screen.
The browser parses HTML into a document structure: elements nested inside other elements, ready to be styled.
Styles tell the browser about sizes, type, spacing and layout. Good hierarchy makes information easier to scan.
JavaScript can respond to input and update what you see. Many pages work with little or no JavaScript.
Layout, painting and compositing turn those instructions into pixels. Smooth motion needs frames delivered on time.
A slow page might wait for data, execute too much code, or spend too long laying out the screen.
Compress what you send. Cache what you can. Prioritize what matters. Design the experience, not just the screenshot.
So the next time a page appears instantly, remember the invisible choreography behind that single click.
